title: Keep them (John 17:6–19)
hook: he prays for his friends: not out of the world, but kept from evil
carry: in the world, but not of it
tomorrow: that they may all be one

segments.voice: Yesterday, he lifted his eyes and said, hora, the hour is come. Your line was this is life eternal: knowing, not just lasting. Who did you get to know a little better? Day six hundred forty.

If you've ever overheard someone praying for you, you know it's a strange and tender thing. A grandmother at the kitchen table who didn't know you'd come in. A parent at the hospital door. A friend who says, I've been praying for you, and means it. You're hearing what they say about you when they're talking to God, not to you. That's what the disciples get at this table. Jesus prays for them out loud, while they're sitting right there. And what he asks for them is not what you might expect.
screen: `THE DISCIPLES HEAR IT AT THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: He begins by describing them, and it's generous. They were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word. These are the same friends who argued about who was greatest, who didn't understand half of what he said, and one of whom will deny him tonight. He talks about them as faithful anyway. Then the center of the prayer: "Holy Father, keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me, that they may be one, as we are." Keep. The Greek word is tereo: to watch over, to guard, to keep safe, the word for a guard keeping watch. And he says that while he was with them, he kept them himself. Now he's leaving, so he hands the job to the Father. Then the line that surprises people: "I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil." He could have asked for an escape. Get them out of here, somewhere safe. He doesn't. He wants them to stay in the middle of things, and be guarded there. Some translations say from the evil one; the Greek can be read either way, as evil or as the evil one, and scholars differ. Then: "Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth." Sanctify means to set apart, make holy. And a few lines later he says, as you sent me into the world, so I've sent them into the world. Not out of the world. Into it. Christians often sum this up with a phrase drawn from these verses: in the world, but not of it.
screen: `NOT OUT OF THE WORLD, BUT KEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for your friends by name. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind three friends, one at a time. Picture each face. Think about where each of them is today: the job, the worry, the place they can't escape. Don't wish them out of it. Wish them kept in it. If you pray, you can say his words over each one, by name: keep them. If you don't, hold each friend in mind for a few breaths and wish them safe where they are. The bell holds the time.
Keep them. Jesus asks the Father to guard his friends, not by taking them out of the world, but by keeping them safe in it.
Your line: in the world, but not of it. Today, send one of those three friends a message: I was thinking of you today. Day six hundred forty.

screen: `DAY 640 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THAT THEY MAY ALL BE ONE.`

howItsDone: Many Christians pray for friends and family by name every day, some with a written list, and intercession, praying for others, is part of almost every Christian service.

myth: Jesus prays for his friends to be taken out of the world
"I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil."
the Greek can be read 'from evil' or 'from the evil one'
translations differ, and so do scholars.
the exact phrase 'in the world but not of it' appears in John 17
it's a summary Christians draw from these verses, not a quotation.

fork.setup: you're praying for friends you're about to leave behind in a dangerous place. what do you ask?
options: take them out of the world, somewhere safe.
keep them from evil, right where they are.
make them strong enough not to need anyone.
fork.reveal: he asks for them to be kept, not removed: not out of the world, but kept from the evil.

original.note: Greek: keep them. tereo means to watch over, to guard, to keep safe.

trapdoor: what you thought: keep them means hold on to them.
what it means: guard them, watch over them, and leave them in the world while you do.
what a scholar hears: tereo, a guard's word, and an ambiguity in 17:15: tou ponerou can mean 'evil' or 'the evil one'.
recall: went out to meet him on the road

sources.quoted: Holy Father, keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me, that they may be one, as we are.
I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil.
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.

notes: 'One of whom will deny him tonight': Peter's denial is predicted in 13:38 and happens in 18:15–27. Confirm wording.
tou ponerou in 17:15: masculine 'the evil one' or neuter 'evil' both possible. Confirm.
'In the world but not of it' is a summary drawn from 17:14–18, not a verse. Confirm.
